sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation in large language models. In each drafting stage, a lightweight draft model proposes tokens that the target model subsequently verifies. With increasingly capable draft models, we find that the target model frequently accepts all tokens produced in a drafting stage. A verification nevertheless follows each drafting stage, resulting in unnecessary target-model forward passes even when drafting could have continued. Adaptive draft length methods decide during decoding how many draft tokens precede a verification, but they raise the speedup only for autoregressive draft models. For a parallel draft model, drafting further requires target-model hidden states for draft tokens that have not been verified. We propose DLoop, a looped form of speculative decoding that adaptively performs multiple drafting stages before verification. DLoop continues drafting while the draft model remains confident and verifies all accumulated draft tokens together. Loop-aware training keeps the draft model reliable in the additional drafting stages by exposing it to its own hidden states for unverified draft tokens. By spending additional draft-model forward passes, DLoop reduces the number of target-model forward passes required for verification. Across diverse speculative decoding methods including EAGLE-3, DFlash, Domino, DSpark, and multi-token prediction modules, DLoop improves the wall-clock speedup by 5 to 41 percent while preserving lossless decoding. Code will be available at https://github.com/naver-ai/DLoop.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) accelerates autoregressive generation in large language models (Brown et al., 2020; Achiam et al., 2023; Team et al., 2023; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2025), where each token costs full forward pass of the model. In each drafting stage, lightweight draft model proposes several draft tokens that the target model is likely to generate next. It produces them either token by token (Li et al., 2024a;b; 2025) or in parallel (Chen et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). The target model then verifies these draft tokens in single forward pass while preserving its output distribution. Speculative decoding performs verification after every drafting stage, even when the draft model could have continued. If the draft model keeps producing tokens that the target model accepts, additional lightweight drafting stages can replace costly verifications. As shown in Fig. 1, across four draft models and three task categories, substantial fraction of drafting stages are fully accepted, that is, every draft token passes verification. Verification also dominates decoding time, since it requires full forward pass of the target model. The latency of that pass, however, grows only modestly with the number of tokens it verifies (Pope et al., 2023). Adaptive draft length methods were proposed to address this problem by deciding during decoding how many draft tokens precede verification (Kim et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025; Mamou et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026; 2024b; Brown et al., 2024). These methods raise the speedup only for autoregressive draft models as shown in Section 4.2. These methods build on an autoregressive draft model, either separate small language model or drafter of the EAGLE family (Li et al., 2024a;b; 2025). Such draft model produces one token at time and can therefore stop or continue drafting at any token. parallel draft model (Chen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026) instead produces all draft tokens of drafting stage in single forward pass. Stopping early leaves the cost of this forward pass unchanged. 1 Preprint. Drafting further requires target-model hidden states for draft tokens that have not been verified. Without them, the draft model conditions on its own hidden states, setting it was not trained for. In this work, we propose DLoop, looped form of speculative decoding in which single verification covers multiple drafting stages. DLoop consists of two components, confidence-gated drafting loop at inference and loopaware training. The drafting loop, illustrated in Fig. 2, decides how many drafting stages single verification covers. It repeats the drafting stage while the draft model remains confident in the draft tokens it has just produced. After each drafting stage, the loop scores this confidence by summing the log probabilities of these draft tokens. If the score remains above threshold, the loop performs an additional drafting stage. Otherwise, the target model verifies all accumulated draft tokens in one forward pass. Since the loop repeats whole drafting stages, it applies to parallel and autoregressive draft models alike. As in standard speculative decoding, the acceptance rule is unchanged and decoding remains lossless. Figure 1: Full acceptance is common. Fraction of drafting stages in which the target model accepts every draft token, under standard speculative decoding with Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) and greedy decoding (T = 0). Loop-aware training aims to keep the draft model reliable in the additional drafting stages. An additional drafting stage conditions on the draft tokens of earlier drafting stages. Target-model hidden states exist only for the tokens before the first drafting stage. Loop-aware training exposes the draft model to its own hidden states for the draft tokens that follow. It is inspired by the training-time test of EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025). That test unrolls the draft model over its own predicted features within one drafting stage. Loop-aware training extends this unrolling across the drafting stages of the loop. Unlike the training-time test, it thus applies to parallel draft models as well. We evaluate DLoop on EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025), DFlash (Chen et al., 2026), Domino (Huang et al., 2026), DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), and multi-token prediction modules (MTP) (Team, 2026a; Team et al., 2026). In every one of these settings, the loop and loop-aware training together raise both the acceptance length and the wall-clock speedup. DLoop obtains this speedup by spending additional draft-model forward passes to reduce the number of target-model forward passes. It does not require additional parameters and applies on top of these publicly released draft models. DLoop does not change how draft model produces tokens, only how many drafting stages precede verification. The number of drafting stages before verification need not be fixed by the schedule and can be decided during decoding.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Speculative decoding. The speedup of speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) depends on the acceptance length and the cost of drafting stage. Early formulations train separate draft model from the same family as the target model, whereas later work builds the draft model on the target model itself. Decoding heads attached to the target model (Stern et al., 2018; Cai et al., 2024) propose several future tokens in parallel from its already computed hidden states. The EAGLE family (Li et al., 2024a;b; 2025) replaces these parallel heads with lightweight autoregressive drafter that conditions on the same hidden states. The multi-token prediction modules released with recent models (Team, 2026a; Team et al., 2026) take the same autoregressive form, feeding each hidden state back to produce the next draft token. EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) trains its drafter with training-time test, which unrolls it over its own predicted features within one drafting stage. Loop-aware training extends that unrolling across the drafting stages that single verification covers. VAT (Gu et al., 2026) instead reshapes the supervision itself, weighting each position by whether it survives simulated verification. The parallel draft models DFlash (Chen et al., 2026), Domino (Huang et al., 2026), and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026) remove the sequential cost of autoregressive drafting by producing whole block in one forward pass. Tree verification broadens what one drafting stage proposes to tree of candidates that the target model verifies together (Miao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Ringel & Romano, 2026; Li et al., 2026). All of 2 Preprint. Figure 2: Comparison of speculative and looped speculative decoding. We assume that the target model accepts all 7 tokens of the first drafting stage and 3 of 7 from the second, 10 tokens in total. The bonus token that each verification produces is omitted for clarity. (a) Speculative decoding verifies after each drafting stage and needs two verifications. (b) Looped speculative decoding skips the first verification because the gate function fgate finds the first drafting stage confident. It then verifies all 14 draft tokens at once and yields the 10 tokens in single verification. Latency is measured with 1,024-token input prefix on single H100 GPU, using Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) as the target model and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026) as the draft model. them change how draft model produces block, whereas DLoop changes only how many blocks precede verification. The same loop therefore runs on EAGLE-3, DFlash, Domino, DSpark, and the multi-token prediction modules. It also composes with tree verification. Adaptive draft length. Most speculative decoding methods fix the length of drafting stage in advance, whereas prior works have explored determining its length dynamically during decoding. BiLD (Kim et al., 2023) and Draft&Verify (Zhang et al., 2024a) stop on the top-1 probability of the draft distribution. SVIP (Zhang et al., 2025) and AdaEDL (Agrawal et al., 2024) stop on its entropy. Dynamic depth decoding (DDD) (Brown et al., 2024) grows the draft tree (Li et al., 2024b) deeper while the summed probability of the sequences in the beam remains above threshold. LLMCad (Xu et al., 2023) accumulates the confidences of the draft tokens within one drafting stage and calls the target model once the accumulated confidence falls below threshold. Our gate function also accumulates confidence over block, but it decides whether further drafting stage should follow. Other methods train module for the decision. SpecDec++ (Huang et al., 2025) predicts the acceptance probability of each draft token, DISCO (Mamou et al., 2024) classifies whether to continue, and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026) sets load-aware verification length from calibrated acceptance probabilities. AdaEAGLE (Zhang et al., 2024b) predicts the length once, before the drafting stage begins. All of them choose where the draft for one verification ends (for DSpark, how much of it is verified), whereas DLoop keeps full drafting stage as the minimum and decides whether another drafting stage follows. PACER (Zhang et al., 2026) drafts autoregressively in blocks and appends another block while separately trained pre-verification layers mean predicted acceptance for the latest block stays above threshold. Unlike PACER, DLoop gates on the confidence of the drafter itself and applies loop-aware training to the drafter. SpecBlock (Shi et al., 2026) trains new draft model that drafts up to fixed number of blocks before verification, and co-trained rank head decides which positions start later block. DLoop instead applies to existing draft models without an additional module.

sections.title: 3 LOOPED SPECULATIVE DECODING
sections.content: 3.1 BACKGROUND Preliminary. Let Mt denote the target model, Md the draft model, and the block size, the number of draft tokens proposed in one drafting stage. Let denote the loop depth, the number of drafting stages that single verification covers. As shown in Fig. 2(a), standard speculative decoding runs one drafting stage (S = 1) and one verification. Drafting starts from prefix x1:t, the input prompt followed by the tokens verified so far, together with two quantities that Mt has produced for it. The first is the anchor token xt, the last token of the prefix, from which the next block is predicted. It is the token that Mt itself produced in the preceding forward pass, commonly referred to as the bonus token. We call it the anchor token when drafting stage starts from it and the bonus token when verification produces it. The second is the target-side context, the hidden states h1:t1 gathered 3 Preprint. from set of layers of Mt, which Md projects to its own hidden size. The context ends at position 1 because Mt has generated the anchor token by next-token prediction but has not yet run forward pass on it. In the drafting stage, Md conditions on the two quantities and proposes block of draft tokens, ˆxt+1:t+k = Md(h1:t1, xt), (1) each with log probability under Md. Existing draft methods differ in how the context is injected and in how the tokens are produced. An autoregressive draft model (Li et al., 2025; Team, 2026a; Team et al., 2026) produces them one at time and drafts each token after the first from its own hidden states. parallel draft model (Chen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026) instead produces all tokens in single forward pass. In the verification, Mt processes the block in single forward pass and applies the acceptance rule of speculative sampling (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). If the first {0, . . . , k} draft tokens are accepted, the verification adds these tokens to the prefix together with bonus token produced by Mt. The hidden states of these positions come from the same pass. The token produced by Mt becomes the anchor token of the next drafting stage. Limitation of fixed verification procedure. We argue that the de facto standard draft-verify procedure is inherently inefficient due to its fixed alternating structure. Specifically, even when all draft tokens are accepted, the next drafting stage must wait for another verification. Thus, one verification yields at most + 1 tokens regardless of how accurately Md drafts. Fig. 1 shows that substantial fraction of blocks reach this bound. This bound is costly because verification requires full forward pass of the target model and dominates decoding time. Adaptive draft length methods (Kim et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026) decide during decoding how many draft tokens precede verification. Section 4.2 shows that they raise the speedup only for autoregressive draft models. For parallel draft model, stopping early leaves the cost of drafting stage unchanged. Drafting further requires target-model hidden states for draft tokens that have not been verified. Our goal is to allow single verification to cover multiple drafting stages. 3.2 CONFIDENCE-GATED DRAFTING LOOP DLoop performs 1 drafting stages and single verification, as shown in Fig. 2(b). The s-th drafting stage produces block ˆxt+(s1)k+1:t+sk. After each drafting stage, gate function decides whether to perform another. When the gate function stops the loop, the target model verifies the accumulated draft tokens ˆxt+1:t+Sk in one forward pass. The gate function decides the number of drafting stages during decoding. Since the loop repeats whole drafting stages, it applies to parallel and autoregressive draft models alike. During training, the first drafting stage receives the hidden states h1:t1 that Mt computed on prefix and is supervised to predict the tokens that follow. EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) unrolls this supervision over the draft models own hidden states for the depth of one drafting stage. Loop-aware training starts from that design. Each additional drafting stage takes the chain of final-layer hidden states that Md computed in the preceding drafting stages, as in the loop. The tokens at these positions come from the ground truth. Training therefore reproduces the chain of hidden states that the loop builds and not the draft tokens that accompany it. The last 5 Preprint. drafting stage predicts the farthest block from the longest chain of and forms the hardest part. We place the second loss term only on the last drafting stage. Every training iteration therefore focuses on this hardest part. The intermediate drafting stages do not contribute to the loss and only supply to the next drafting stage. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENT
sections.content: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP We evaluate DLoop on four draft models, EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025), DFlash (Chen et al., 2026), Domino (Huang et al., 2026), and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), with Qwen3-4B and Qwen38B (Yang et al., 2025) as target models. We also evaluate DLoop with the MTP modules released with Qwen3.5-9B (Team, 2026a) and Gemma-4-12B (Team et al., 2026). The block size is 16 for DFlash and Domino, 7 for DSpark, 3 for MTP with Qwen3.5-9B, and 6 for MTP with Gemma-412B. Loop-aware training starts from the released official weights of each draft model and runs for one epoch. Following prior works (Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026), we construct the training set from the 1.3 million user prompts of PerfectBlend (Xu et al., 2024) paired with responses regenerated by each target model with its recommended sampling parameters. All training hyperparameters follow those released with each method. Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods (Team, 2026a; Team et al., 2026) do not provide recipe for training only the MTP modules. For these methods, we therefore use the training recipe of EAGLE-3. EAGLE-3 has no officially released weights for these target models. We therefore train EAGLE-3 draft models for three epochs on the same data and use them as the baseline draft model. We follow the evaluation protocol of DFlash1, detailed in Appendix A.1, and evaluate on eight benchmarks in three task categories, math (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024), AIME25), code (HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), LiveCodeBench (LCB) (Jain et al., 2025)), and chat (MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023), Alpaca (Taori et al., 2023)). We report the acceptance length τ , the average number of tokens accepted per verification, and the wall-clock speedup over autoregressive decoding. All results use greedy decoding (T = 0) unless stated otherwise. For tree verification, we apply DDTree (Ringel & Romano, 2026) to DFlash and DARTree (Li et al., 2026) to Domino and DSpark. We follow the maximum number of node budget in the tree that the target model verifies from their papers: 256 for DFlash, 64 for Domino and DSpark. EAGLE-3 uses its own tree verification with the released setting. We sweep the gate threshold over {0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0}, as detailed in the appendix Tab. A5 and select the value with the highest average speedup over the eight benchmarks. We use 0.5 for all settings, except EAGLE-3 with Qwen3-8B, where we use 0.75. All training and evaluation runs use NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs with bf16 precision. 4.2 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS DLoop on recent draft models Table 1 reports the results for the four draft models with Qwen34B and Qwen3-8B, and for MTP with Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma-4-12B. For the autoregressive draft models, which already draft each token after the first from their own hidden states, both the acceptance length and the speedup improve for EAGLE-3 with both target models and for MTP with Qwen3.5-9B. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced DLoop, looped form of speculative decoding in which single verification covers multiple drafting stages. The confidence-gated drafting loop repeats the drafting stage while the draft model remains confident. Loop-aware training keeps the draft model reliable in the additional drafting stages by exposing it to its own hidden states for unverified draft tokens. DLoop leaves the architecture of the draft model and the acceptance rule unchanged. It changes only how many drafting stages precede verification. Across EAGLE-3, DFlash, Domino, DSpark, and multi-token prediction modules, DLoop improves the wall-clock speedup by 5 to 41 percent while preserving 9 Preprint. lossless decoding. It obtains this speedup by spending additional draft-model forward passes to reduce the number of target-model forward passes. Adaptive draft length methods raise the speedup only for autoregressive draft models, whereas DLoop raises it for parallel draft models as well. The ablation shows that loop-aware training prepares the draft model for the loop rather than improving each drafting stage on its own. Applied on top of tree verification, DLoop further raises the acceptance length and the speedup. These results show that the number of drafting stages before verification need not be fixed by the schedule and can be decided during decoding. 10 Preprint.

Appendix A.5 measures the time and the peak GPU memory of one loop by the number of drafting stages. Appendix A.6 presents representative generations of the confidence-gated drafting loop. Appendix A.7 compares design choices for the gate threshold, the gate function, and loop-aware training. Appendix A.8 details how we apply the adaptive draft length methods to EAGLE-3 and DSpark. A.1 EVALUATION PROTOCOL The eight benchmarks and their sample counts follow the official DFlash evaluation code. Table A1 lists the source and the number of evaluated samples for each benchmark. DLoop raises the acceptance length on every benchmark for every draft model and target model. The gain is largest on math and smallest on chat. The full acceptance ratio in Fig. 1 follows the same order. Table A10 reports the same settings with sampling at temperature = 1. At = 1, DLoop also raises the average acceptance length. A.3 SERVING THROUGHPUT UNDER CONCURRENCY. Table A2 evaluates DLoop with both DFlash and DSpark in SGLang under concurrent serving with Qwen3-8B as the target model. DLoop improves throughput substantially at low concurrency. On MATH-500 at = 1, the speedup increases from 5.81 to 6.23 with DFlash and from 4.45 to 4.94 with DSpark, with similar gains on HumanEval. The gain generally becomes smaller as concurrency increases, but DLoop remains beneficial through = 8 with DFlash and through = 16 14 Preprint. with DSpark on both benchmarks. At = 32, DFlash+DLoop slightly underperforms DFlash, whereas DSpark+DLoop continues to improve throughput on MATH-500 and remains within 1% of DSpark on HumanEval. This attenuation is consistent with the known interaction between speculative decoding and batching, in which additional speculative work consumes increasingly scarce batch capacity as the target model becomes saturated, reducing the optimal speculation depth at high load (Su et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024b; Cheng et al., 2026). DLoop further chooses the number of drafting stages independently for each sample, yielding ragged draft-side execution whose efficient batching requires either padding, which wastes computation, or dynamic regrouping, which introduces additional scheduling overhead. Such sample-dependent execution therefore leaves room for serving and kernel optimizations that better support adaptive loop depths. Overall, DLoop retains substantial throughput gains at low-to-moderate concurrency, while its advantage diminishes as serving becomes increasingly batch-bound. BiLD, SVIP, AdaEDL, and LLMCad stop drafting once statistic of the draft distribution crosses threshold. BiLD uses the top-1 probability, whereas SVIP and AdaEDL use the entropy. LLMCad uses the confidence accumulated over the draft tokens. AdaEDL and LLMCad also adjust the threshold after each verification according to how many draft tokens were accepted. DDD applies similar rule to the draft tree of EAGLE-2, checking the summed probability of the sequences in the beam at preset depths. SpecDec++ and DISCO instead train head that decides after each draft token whether to stop. AdaEAGLE trains predictor that sets the draft length once, before the drafting stage begins. PACER drafts in blocks of tokens (b is set to each draft models draft length) and trains pre-verification layer. It drafts another block while the mean acceptance that this layer predicts for the latest block remains above threshold. The confidence scheduler of DSpark chooses how many draft tokens of the full block to verify, using confidence head trained together with DSpark. The scheduler therefore does not apply to EAGLE-3. A.8.2 APPLICATION TO EAGLE-3. BiLD, SVIP, AdaEDL, LLMCad, SpecDec++, DISCO, and PACER were proposed for separate small autoregressive LLM as the draft model. EAGLE-3 instead expands its draft tree by one depth per forward pass. We evaluate each rule after every depth on the highest-scoring path of the tree and stop the expansion once the rule stops drafting. PACER runs its pre-verification layer on the same path after every draft tokens. DDD checks the beam at the preset depths of its paper. We run each rule with the default maximum depth of EAGLE-3 and with the maximum draft length of its paper. We port the fallback policy of BiLD and omit its rollback policy. The rollback policy replaces lossless verification with rule that can change the output of the target model. A.8.3 APPLICATION TO DSPARK. The parallel draft model DSpark computes all draft tokens of drafting stage in single forward pass. Every method except PACER and DDD evaluates its rule on the full block. Only the draft tokens before the position where the rule stops go to verification. For AdaEAGLE, the predicted length sets the number of verified draft tokens. Discarding the remaining draft tokens shortens only the verification. With Qwen3-4B on single H100 GPU at batch size 1, verification takes 22.2 0.3 ms for any number of draft tokens from 2 to 16. When rule does not stop within the block, we also let it perform another drafting stage, up to the maximum draft length of its paper. PACER and DDD instead decide at the end of each drafting stage whether another drafting stage follows. All additional drafting stages use the publicly released weights of DSpark and take the input of Eq. 3. Since DSpark drafts single chain, the criterion of DDD becomes the sum of the log probabilities of all draft tokens after the anchor token. It differs from our gate function only in accumulating over drafting stages. 18 Preprint. A.8.4 TRAINING AND TUNING. We train the decision heads of SpecDec++, DISCO, AdaEAGLE, and PACER for one epoch on the same data as loop-aware training. Their architecture, inputs, labels, and loss follow the original papers. We keep the other constants of each rule from its paper and sweep its threshold, together with for PACER. Table 3 reports, for each method, the setting with the highest average speedup. Preprint.
